Check What an Optimizer Reports

Source: R/check_optimizer.R
check_optimizer.Rd

Puts an optimizer through twelve checks on what it reports, prints the verdict on each, and then runs it over the standard test problems and reports the gap that it reached on each one. It is intended for a caller who adds a method. Every shipped method except brent() passes all twelve checks; brent() minimizes a function of one variable and cannot run the battery, whose problems have more parameters.

Usage

check_optimizer(
  optimizer,
  problems = test_problems(),
  verbose = TRUE,
  tol = 1e-06
)

Arguments

optimizer

The optimizer() to check. Anything else raises an error naming bfgs() as an example.

problems

A list of problems in the shape that test_problems() returns. Defaults to every problem of test_problems(). Pass a subset to keep the report short: test_problems("sphere").

verbose

TRUE (default) prints the twelve verdicts and the battery table; FALSE returns the same information silently.

tol

Tolerance for the checks that compare numbers, a single positive number, default 1e-6. It applies to check 1 and to the comparison of the two values in check 9. Check 2 uses a fixed 1e-3 on the gradient, check 9 compares the two points with a fixed relative tolerance of 1e-5, check 12 uses a fixed 1e-3 on the distance to the solution, and check 7 tests the bounds strictly, without a tolerance.

Value

Invisibly, a named list of two:

checks

a named logical vector of length 12, one entry per numbered check, named by what the check asserts.

battery

a data frame with one row per problem and the columns problem, value, gap, converged, evaluations and note. A problem that the optimizer could not run keeps its name in problem, has NA in the other numeric and logical columns, and has the error message in note.

Requirements and performance

The twelve numbered checks are statements that an optimizer must satisfy whatever its performance. The performance comes afterwards, as a table of gaps without a verdict. The two are kept apart because a slow method can satisfy every requirement: gradient descent does not solve Rosenbrock in five hundred iterations, which is a documented property of the method.

The only performance requirement among the numbered checks is check 12, the minimization of a quadratic, which every correct method passes.

The twelve checks

  1. value is the objective at par. A method that reports the value at a point that it has since left passes every test that uses only the value.

  2. the reported gradient is the gradient at par. The check is run only for an optimizer that declares "gradient" through optimizer_provides(). bundle() reports an aggregate subgradient and does not declare a gradient, so the check does not apply to it.

  3. converged follows the stopping rule and is never inferred from the run having ended. The check starves the optimizer of iterations, and a run cut off after one iteration must not report success.

  4. budgets are respected: iterations never exceeds maxit.

  5. evaluations are counted: the reported number of evaluations is not zero.

  6. the trace, when kept, is a data frame whose key column (iteration, or start for a multistart() trace) starts at one and increases.

  7. bounds are respected strictly. A probability of exactly 1 is not a probability inside \((0, 1)\), and the next computation of the caller often divides by it.

  8. the run repeats. A deterministic method gives the same answer twice; a stochastic one gives it again from the seed that it recorded, which tests the recording as well as the repeatability.

  9. maximize() is minimize() of the negative.

  10. a stopping rule that the optimizer cannot evaluate is rejected when the run starts, and is not accepted and left never to fire.

  11. a starting point where the objective is not finite raises an error, so that a run does not return NaN silently.

  12. it minimizes a quadratic.

An optimizer that returns an invented point with converged = TRUE fails six of the twelve checks: 1, 2, 3, 10, 11 and 12. The six that it passes concern bookkeeping.

The problem battery

The table reports the gap between the value reached and the known minimum, as information. A large gap on rastrigin or himmelblau means the method found a different local minimum, which for a local method is correct behavior, and the note column labels those two. A large gap on abs_sum means that the method stopped at a kink, the case for which bundle() and the derivative-free methods are intended.

See also

test_problems() for the battery, check_criterion() and check_bounds() for the two functions that a new method has to call, optimizer_provides() for the declaration read by check 2.

Examples

check_optimizer(bfgs())
#> Checking optimizer: BFGS
#>   [ 1] value agrees with par:                       [PASSED]
#>   [ 2] gradient agrees with par:                    [PASSED]
#>   [ 3] convergence is not assumed:                  [PASSED]
#>   [ 4] budgets are respected:                       [PASSED]
#>   [ 5] evaluations are counted:                     [PASSED]
#>   [ 6] trace is well formed:                        [PASSED]
#>   [ 7] bounds are respected strictly:               [PASSED]
#>   [ 8] the run repeats:                             [PASSED]
#>   [ 9] maximize mirrors minimize:                   [PASSED]
#>   [10] a rule that cannot be evaluated is rejected: [PASSED]
#>   [11] a bad starting point is an error:            [PASSED]
#>   [12] it minimizes a quadratic:                    [PASSED]
#> 
#>   All checks passed.
#> 
#>   battery (gap from the known minimum; information, not a verdict)
#>     sphere       gap  4.62e-33  conv        3 evals  
#>     rosenbrock   gap  3.23e-13  conv       49 evals  
#>     booth        gap  1.73e-17  conv        8 evals  
#>     beale        gap  3.18e-15  conv       17 evals  
#>     powell       gap  4.28e-11  conv       39 evals  
#>     himmelblau   gap  6.27e-14  conv       17 evals  multimodal
#>     rastrigin    gap  0.00e+00  conv       11 evals  multimodal
#>     abs_sum      gap  1.26e-02  -          84 evals  non-smooth

# For a method that computes no gradient, the gradient check does not
# apply, and the other checks are the same.
res <- check_optimizer(nelder_mead(), problems = test_problems("sphere"))
#> Checking optimizer: nelder-mead
#>   [ 1] value agrees with par:                       [PASSED]
#>   [ 2] gradient agrees with par:                    [PASSED]
#>   [ 3] convergence is not assumed:                  [PASSED]
#>   [ 4] budgets are respected:                       [PASSED]
#>   [ 5] evaluations are counted:                     [PASSED]
#>   [ 6] trace is well formed:                        [PASSED]
#>   [ 7] bounds are respected strictly:               [PASSED]
#>   [ 8] the run repeats:                             [PASSED]
#>   [ 9] maximize mirrors minimize:                   [PASSED]
#>   [10] a rule that cannot be evaluated is rejected: [PASSED]
#>   [11] a bad starting point is an error:            [PASSED]
#>   [12] it minimizes a quadratic:                    [PASSED]
#> 
#>   All checks passed.
#> 
#>   battery (gap from the known minimum; information, not a verdict)
#>     sphere       gap  2.14e-17  conv      276 evals  
all(res$checks)
#> [1] TRUE

# The battery is returned as a table.
check_optimizer(cg(), verbose = FALSE)$battery
#>      problem        value          gap converged evaluations       note
#> 1     sphere 0.000000e+00 0.000000e+00      TRUE           3           
#> 2 rosenbrock 7.399642e-10 7.399642e-10      TRUE         249           
#> 3      booth 1.010522e-11 1.010522e-11      TRUE          73           
#> 4      beale 1.116830e-11 1.116830e-11      TRUE         100           
#> 5     powell 1.048119e-07 1.048119e-07      TRUE         549           
#> 6 himmelblau 1.754022e-11 1.754022e-11      TRUE          97 multimodal
#> 7  rastrigin 0.000000e+00 0.000000e+00      TRUE          60 multimodal
#> 8    abs_sum 4.504423e-02 4.504423e-02      TRUE         146 non-smooth
